title: Designed for the second deployment
angle: AI into an unglamorous service business. Cycle time, error rate and unit cost against a named baseline — and our own weakest column named in minute 4 instead of lost in Q&A.
endline: Don't trust the AI. Trust the manual.

marks.do: mt-07 → 2018 → Yes. Put the phone DOWN.
The diagram. Three zone labels only. 90 s.
Chat → chain is loose, what do I do → tap a chip.
THE CAR. civic → tire pressure → flat tyre. Never cut this.
The MT-07 is ready. Type oil. "Nobody touched it."
The honest column. Say it flat, then the plan.
Back to the marked page. Close.

slides.label: A motorcycle workshop in Germany
slides.sub: a year, per mechanic, *looking for a page*. That is his number — and *EUR 36–48k* of billable time is arithmetic on his number.
notes: *One person, not a market.* "A friend of mine." Not "shops everywhere", not "the $X billion repair industry". Long Lake buys individual businesses; they think in units of one company, and so should you.
Say the 400 hours, then stop for two seconds.
Say ~he says~ and ~that's arithmetic on his number~ out loud. Do not quote a TAM — we have no sourced one.

defs.d: 20% × 2,000 h — arithmetic on his number and an assumed 2,000-hour year (computed).
share of his working time spent looking for a page — HIS estimate (assumed). Always say "he says".
400 h × EUR 90–120/h (computed).

slides.kicker: He does not use AI. Two reasons, both fair.

items.label: right — and he signs for the 5%
items.sub: A wrong torque figure is not a wrong paragraph. It is a wheel that comes off.

items.label: a question, when he tried it
items.sub: The model had to read a 500-page manual. He hit his limit before lunch.

notes: *These are his objections, not your argument.* You are agreeing with a skeptic, in a room full of people whose job is installing AI into businesses run by exactly this kind of skeptic.
If you have thirty spare seconds anywhere, spend them here: ~the hardest part of the FDE job you're hiring for is this guy, and he's right.~
Do not blend his ~$4 with our $12.40 — different measurements of different manuals.

defs.d: his line, quoted: "95% right isn't enough when I sign for the 5%." His number, not ours.
what one question cost him when he tried an LLM — HIS bill (assumed).

slides.title: Built once. Deployed N times.
slides.caption: A vehicle nobody has asked for yet becomes a searchable manual on its own — and the next shop inherits it.
notes: *Seven boxes, ninety seconds, three things only:* eighty-four publisher portals with no API behind that registry; nine cents and forty seconds per new vehicle, with no human in it; zero engineering per new shop, because the loop comes back to the same registry.

If they lean in, give them the Ducati / Kawasaki / Honda war stories — an operator who has integrated a legacy ERP recognises that suffering instantly, and it is the fastest credibility you will get all day.
"The second deployment is the only one that matters, and it is already cheaper than the first."

slides.title: The answer is a page
slides.line: KTM's page 77, and the marker sits on the two lines that answer him.
points: "If we can't find the ink, we don't draw the marker."
Five minutes of thumbing a PDF became two seconds.
That is the cycle time, and it is the whole product.
notes: *This is the slide. Stop talking.* Let them read the marked line.

Then one sentence: ~it's only there because we found that exact text in KTM's PDF — if we can't find the ink, we don't draw the marker.~ That sentence is the entire trust story; everything else is convenience.
The car moment comes next. Do not oversell it — type `civic`, tap it, ask, open the page, then: ~nobody wrote a car version.~ It lands harder if you're bored by it.

notes: *Say the two numbers and shut up.* Do not say "thirty-two thousand times cheaper". Say "twelve dollars forty" and "six ten-thousandths of a dollar" and let them divide. Operators trust arithmetic they did themselves.
Cycle time, error rate, unit cost — that is their bullet #4, in their order.
Never quote the live ledger without the timestamp. It moved $8.08 → $8.93 in thirteen minutes on the day these files were written.

slides.text: This is not in daily production use. One shop. One mechanic. Zero installs, no adoption data.
slides.sub: *Ten independent shops for one month*, and the only number I care about is how much of that twenty percent comes back. Everything you'd need to measure it is already logged per route.
notes: *Deliver the weakness flat, then immediately give the plan.* Do not apologise, do not hedge with "but".

"This is not in daily production use. Here's what I'd do about it: ten shops, one month, and the number is how much of the twenty percent comes back." The plan is what turns the concession into a credential.
This being the last slide is deliberate. In this room, the team that puts its own weakest column on the final slide is the team that gets believed about the other five.
Then the close, back on the marked page: ~there is not one AI-written sentence on it. The model never gets to be the answer — it only gets to point.~

slides.title: long-lake.md — check this list the morning of

groups.label: This pitch
items: Do not claim installs, adoption or throughput data: one design partner, zero installs. That is the deduction you name yourself.
Do not quote a TAM — we have no sourced one.
Do not lead with a multiple. Lead with $12.40 and $0.0006 and let them divide.
Do not demo anything pending a key. Do not say the word Elastic.
Cut in this order if short: the chat at 2:20, then the diagram. NEVER cut the car at 2:45.

groups.label: All nine, global
items: ElevenLabs voice is never "live" — "built, one key away". The live voice is Deepgram.
The 3D backdrop is a technical grid. No panorama, no photographic workshop scene.
Dropbox folder sync and Climate Fit are "built, deploying", not deployed.
Never quote a running ledger total without the date beside it.
Never call 13,537 "manuals" — it is vehicles carrying a free manual. Distinct fetchable PDFs is 14,770.
There is no checkout. "Live prices", never "buy".

notes: Presenter-only. The audience sees the end card.
